utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please. And for the record, I note that the Bench is again fully constituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Alex Demirdjian on behalf the Prosecutor, with senior trial attorney Joanna Korner, and Case Manager Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Dominic Kennedy, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Would you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may sit down. Good morning to you, sir, and welcome to the Tribunal. You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution in this trial against Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin, who you'll see to your left. Let me start out by asking you to give us your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Obren Petrovic, born on 11th of May, 1957, in Doboj, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And happy birthday for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What is your profession today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Head of the Doboj municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what was your occupation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Chief of the Doboj Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Petrovic, have you ever testified before this Tribunal or before any domestic tribunal about the crimes that were committed in the course of the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Let me then explain to you briefly how this is going to then proceed. You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution, and I believe that you have met with Mr. Demirdjian already. The Prosecution has asked for four hours for you to testify in chief. After that, the Defence for Mr. Stanisic has asked for five hours, and the Defence for Mr. Zupljanin has asked only for 15 minutes. So this means that your testimony will run for today and tomorrow at least. We normally sit in sessions of 90 minutes because the tapes of the recordings of these proceedings have to be changed every 90 minutes, so we'll have a break at 10.25. The breaks are of 20 minutes' duration. After the Defence has completed their cross-examination, the Prosecution again will be given the floor to examine you in redirect examination, and thereafter the Judges may have some questions for you. If at any time, sir, you feel like you would wish to have a break or have questions, then please do not hesitate to let us know. The proceedings are being translated into English and French, apart from Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian, which means that you have interpreters sitting around us trying to interpret everything we say in this courtroom. Especially when you are being cross-examined by the Defence, you will then, both of you, speak the same language and there's a natural tendency to overlap and to speak very fast when you were in a direct dialogue, but, sir, may I remind you to please observe at all times a break between question and answer because otherwise the interpreters will be unable to follow what you are saying and then your testimony will all be in vain. So help us and help the interpreters to enable them to understand what you are saying. And finally, I remind you of your solemn declaration, and I should also remind you that there's a severe penalty for providing false or incomplete information to the Tribunal. That's all I have to say, and I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petrovic. In answer to the Honourable Judge you stated that you were the head of Doboj municipality. In essence does that mean you are the mayor of the town?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And since when are you the mayor of Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to go through your background, education and professional background. Is it correct that you completed your military service?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And which year was that?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: In 1977 and 1978 in the reserve school for officers in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: After your military service, you finished your studies in 1980; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: In 1980, I finished the teacher's college in Tuzla, and in 1988, the Faculty of Political Sciences in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: After you finished your teacher's college education, you worked for the Territorial Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: From 1980 to 1982 I worked in the professional services as the officer for national defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he did after 1982. The interpreters didn't catch that, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch what you said after 1982. Can you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Between 1982 and 1989, I worked in the Doboj Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was your role in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I worked for two years as the officer for operations and training. And then in 1984 until 1986 I was the assistant chief for intelligence. And then from 1987 to 1989 I was the chief of security of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And you already mentioned that you studied political science in Zagreb from 1986 to 1988. And it is in 1989 that you started to work at the SUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I started working for the state security service, and I remained there until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Right. And this is when you become the head of the SUP in Doboj, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 I became chief of the public security station in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Which month was that in 1991?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: June.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you remained in this position until when?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Until the end of 1992 when I was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you were appointed as chief of the SUP in June 1991, who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: My superior was the chief of the centre Andrija Bjelosovic, as well as the minister of interior according to the hierarchy who was at the time Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you explain to us how you were nominated to the position of chief of the SUP in June 1991?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: After the 1990 elections, an inter-party agreement was reached between the SDA, SDS, and the HDZ; and according to this division, a Serb was to be appointed chief of the station, and the commander was to be from the SDA, and the HDZ was to take up the post of the chief for traffic. After that, the party concerned nominated several candidates, so the number one candidate was Milan Ninkovic, followed by Zoran Zekic, and the third was Zoran Blagojevic. And after lengthy debate, they nominated me as the third candidate because I wasn't a member of the SDS. So these three candidates were put forward as proposals to the BH MUP, and after that I was nominated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the official appointment came from whom?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Minister Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You were the chief of the SUP; who was the commander in the SUP in Doboj at that time in June 1991?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Irfan Hadzic was the commander. And the commander of the traffic police was Mirko Grujic, a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in the SUP you also had a section for crime prevention. How many staff members did you have in that section?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: That was for general crime. There were eight people in the section, and Mladen Bulic was the head of the section.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 6, line 17, I believe your question was recorded as part of the answer of the witness. Maybe this can be remedied.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Page 6, line 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I think your -- your question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- "And the official appointment came from whom;" that was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Thank you for that, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the crime prevention section in the SUP; was there also a crime prevention section in the CSB in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. They were involved in serious crime, white collar crime, and/or other serious criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know who headed that section in the CSB?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Pejo Krnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And are you aware of how many staff members he had under him?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think over 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a small procedural question as we will be seeing a number of documents this morning. Can you tell the Court what was the policy on signatures in the police. Who was authorised to sign documents in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if we are talking about a station, the chief of station is authorised to sign. However, if we are talking about a specific line of work, for example, CAD, then the head of that section can sign information requested by the centre. If it had to do with the administrative section, it was the head of the section. When we talk about prosecutor's office and chief of different sections would sign a proposal and file criminal reports to the prosecutor and, as I said, heads of these sections would normally sign this kind of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Page 7, line 22, you talk about a section; it was recorded as CAD. Can you tell us what that is, or if those letters are correct, actually?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It stands for criminal investigation department. So it should be section then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the criminal investigation section exists as the level of the centre, as I explained. When we talk about the administrative section, it dealt with issuing identity cards, passports, driver's licences, and, of course, they also submitted their own reports to the centre. The centre also had its own administrative department which dealt with these same issues like identity papers and passports and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And you were saying that the heads of the sections were signing the documents when they were drafting it; whose name would appear on those documents in the signature block?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes that would be the name of the chief of station and his name would be put.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the chief of that -- sorry, who would be signing it? Would it be the chief of the section or the chief of the station?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, it could have been signed by the chief of station, but in practice it was done by the head of the criminal investigation section if it had to do with filing a criminal report against an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the political developments in Doboj in 1991. And, first of all, I'd like to ask you whether you -- you told us that you were not -- actually, no. Let me first ask you this, because you told us that you were proposed by the SDS. Were you a member of that party in 1991?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you join the SDS eventually?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, towards the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Therefore in 1991 and in 1992 you were not a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of meetings held by the SDS in Doboj in 1991 which were attended by the leadership of the SDS? Were you aware of those?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I wasn't invited to attend. Had I been invited, I would have known if there were any meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I understand you were not invited, but had you heard of such meetings being held? Had you heard of some members of the leadership attending sessions in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you remind us who was the head of the SDS in Doboj, president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Milan Ninkovic was the president of the SDS in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you know at the time in 1991 of decisions or declarations issued by the SDS in relation to Doboj territory and in relation to the independence of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard -- people talked about that in 1991 and in 1992. It was discussed in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was extensively covered by the media as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in Doboj, what was the substance of those declarations generally? What was the gist of the message of the SDS in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1991 they probably discussed it at length. But after 1991 declaration of Republika Srpska, I think, on the 9th of January and then on the 26th of March, the declaration of the Serbian municipality of Doboj, as I heard, negotiations started between the SDS and the SDA about the problems that existed in the area of Doboj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, what kind of problems existed at the time in Doboj? I'm talking about the end of 1991, early 1992.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The situation was tense. There was ethnic tension as by that time the war in Croatia had broken out. Still there were a lot of discussions going on among these parties, the SDA and SDS, and then in 1991 -- 1992 there were problems about the withdrawal of the JNA and there were frequent meetings between the police and the JNA on the issue of joint patrols that were to protect the army as they were moving in the direction of the Krajina and then onwards, pulling out of the Krajina itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you are saying there were discussions among the parties; what were the proposals that were advocated at the time with regards to these problems?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I heard, and I wasn't present at these meetings, the SDS and the SDA discussed the issue of dividing up the town into two parts. But I think that it all came to nothing; nothing came out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you know who proposed splitting the town?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the reasons behind the establishment of Republika Srpska. Probably there were discussions about the -- among the parties at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the result was the setting up of Republika Srpska and of the Serbian municipality of Doboj, and, of course, they could not have existed as Serbian municipality of Doboj and the municipality of Doboj at once. A solution was sought in that direction therefore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Demirdjian, do you realise that you are examining about adjudicated facts 1266?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in front of me right here, but I'm trying to get -- to develop on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petrovic, you were telling us about problems in the municipality of Doboj. Were you aware of occurrences of properties being blown up?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to whom did these properties or buildings belong to?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Most of them belonged to non-Serbs, i.e., Bosniaks, Albanians, and perhaps Croats, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And were the perpetrators of these acts identified at the time?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think they were for any of these acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were there any suspects, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was within the competence of the Security Services Centre. To my knowledge, not a single perpetrator was uncovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if any investigations were conducted by the Security Services Centre?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On-site investigations took place, but as far as I know, the perpetrators were not identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that this was under the competence of the Security Services Centre. Can you explain that to the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that we had the criminal investigation service which dealt with general crime, i.e., criminal offences that were not as serious; whereas the CSB had more staff, more qualified people. They had the required forensics equipment and staff and was capable of doing the job professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And with regards to blowing up buildings and property, did that require a certain type of experience in that domain?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And who, to your knowledge, would have that sort of experience?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: There were individuals from the army and the MUP who were involved in uncovering subversive activities. They were the ones who could uncover that. And then there were also the ones who set up these explosives had to have been qualified to do so. Not everyone can set an explosive under a car, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So the average citizen wouldn't be able to set up this type of explosives?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, only those who were trained to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In early 1992, could you tell us if there was an issue with the television repeaters in and around Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 the repeater was -- the repeater near Doboj was taken over, and I think it was organised by Major Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say that the repeater was taken, what happened to the repeater?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the repeater was taken and it was the repeater of TV Sarajevo, of the television of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I happened to be on the team who, together with a group of people from Sarajevo, toured the repeater. We found people in camouflage uniform up there who searched us. The people who came from Sarajevo had to repair the repeater because it would not have been operational at all. Those people who were there in camouflage uniform didn't know how to handle it at all, and it would not have been a service to anyone, to either the TV in Sarajevo or to TV Belgrade to be transmitted via that repeater.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what happened when the TV repeater was seised by these men in uniform? Was -- did that have any effect in any way in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: When the repeater was taken, one could no longer watch TV Sarajevo, rather, what it transmitted was TV Belgrade. Later on, the minister of the interior, Delimustafic, visited Doboj and he spoke to the leadership of the SDS and to the leadership of Doboj municipality. I don't recall whether an agreement was reached, a compromise of some sort. In other words, he was there both as a minister and as a representative of the BH government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us that this was organised by Major Stankovic. What was the reaction of the municipal leaders?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The president of the municipality was an SDA member at the time. Of course, the municipality reacted to it, but the Serbian Democratic Party issued a press release at the time where it was stated that the citizens of Doboj of Serb ethnicity wanted to be able to watch TV Belgrade rather than TV Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In relation to Major Stankovic, can you tell us, first of all, his full name?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Milovan Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And at that time which unit did he belong to? And we're talking about early 1992.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: In early 1992 it wasn't generally known which unit he belonged to. He, I believe, belonged to some sort of security intelligence service of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was he from Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. He was from Modrica, near Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us he was from the security intelligence service of the JNA. Was he stationed in Doboj prior to 1992, or ...

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think that he appeared in 1991. We had an army contingent and barracks in Doboj which had its commander and despite that he started forming units in town and its surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You said that he appeared in 1991. Where did he come from, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He was known as Major Stankovic, so he must have been somewhere in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you are saying that he started forming units despite the fact that there was an army contingent in the barracks in Doboj. Can you tell us who was the head of that army contingent in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The commander was Cazim, and I can't remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you remember if Stankovic visited the CSB building in the early 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you know if the head of the CSB ever met with Stankovic in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the municipality of Doboj was declared on the 26th of March, 1992. I'd like to ask you if you are aware of any meetings attended by Andrija Bjelosevic with other high-ranking members of the MUP? I'm talking about prior to May 1992.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And were you informed of -- again, early 1992, of the establishment of a Serb MUP in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't informed of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were there any meetings held in the MUP in Doboj in the CSB? Were there any talks about the creation of this Serb MUP?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I know that a meeting took place. Now, I don't know if it was in March or April. It was held in the hall of the station's building. I know that the meeting was of all the employees, but I don't know what the subject of discussions was. It must have been related to the problems arising at the time. Voting was taking place, or perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure, the elections or what.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I know that there was talk of this Serb MUP being in the making. I don't know what the upshot of the meeting was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, were you present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you hear how many staff members attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think at least 100 people were present, Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And after this meeting, what did you hear about the meeting? What were the reactions?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what it was they discussed. I probably did know at the time. I just can't remember now what it was and why the discussions were so heated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you know anyone who was present during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know many. A relative of mine, a policeman, attended the meeting. So back in 1992 I probably knew what it was they discussed, it's just that I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us a moment ago that this was in relation to the creation of this Serb MUP. Did you hear what was said about the creation of the MUP; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you aware that at the end of March 1992 a dispatch arrived signed by Momcilo Mandic discussing the creation of this Serb MUP?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You don't remember receiving a dispatch of that nature?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We now come to the events in relation to the take-over of Doboj. Can you tell us when that took place?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It happened between the 2nd and the 3rd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How did you come to learn about it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I came to know about it in the following way: On the 3rd of May, I was told that I should go to the SUP because the Red Berets had taken over the public security station building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you go to the public security station?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what did you see upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: As I arrived there, I saw the policemen securing the station. This is what I found out: When the Red Berets got to the SUP that night, they arrested the Bosniak and Croat members of the police and put them into prison, and the Serb policemen were left behind to guard the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned the Red Berets. Had you heard about them before the 3rd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you aware in any way when they arrived in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I heard that they had arrived in April.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last word the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last part of your answer. You said they arrived in April and then ... can you continue? They didn't your answer.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: To Mount Ozren near Doboj; that's where they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think from Serbia, by helicopter. That's -- that was the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if they had a leader?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And who was their leader?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Rajo Bozovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you said that they arrived in Mount Ozren. Where were they stationed?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think up at Petrovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just for the benefit of Trial Chamber, can you tell us where Petrovo is in relation to Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It is in the direction of Tuzla. And before the war, it was part of Gracanica municipality. Because on the way from Doboj to Tuzla, there is the Gracanica municipality, and that's where Petrovo is. And Mount Ozren is between the rivers of Spreca and Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us that the Red Berets took over on -- between the night of the 2nd and 3rd of May. Were any other units present during this take-over?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think that their primary task was to seise SUP, and I think they did it on their own. Later on, in the morning, they engaged detachments with tanks and the army because the SUP building is in the centre of town and the old part of town where -- populated by Bosniaks had not been taken over yet. So later on, on the 3rd, they proceeded to attack Stari Grad, that's to say, the old town of Doboj, "carsija," and that's when the detachments and the army got involved as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what you mean by the detachments. You told us about the Red Berets, you're telling us the army. What are the detachments?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Stankovic formed these detachments in the town proper as well as on the hills surrounding and overlooking Doboj, Mount Ozren, Trebiva [phoen], Krnin [phoen]. Every hill or mount had its own detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And these detachments were made of whom exactly? Who were members of these detachments?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The members were Serbs. Stankovic organised them and appointed commanders of detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how did he select these men?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge were they locals from Doboj or were they from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The detachments consisted of the locals. They took weapons from the army and distributed them among these locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And were there police units from other areas present in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Shortly after the take-over on the 2nd and the 3rd, the unit from Banja Luka arrived, and Martic's police arrived soon thereafter as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, may I ask -- can I ask a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Stankovic that organised the detachments, there is a Stankovic who is deputy mayor of Doboj. Is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now? You mean deputy mayor now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. He styled himself as the commander of the defence of town, and that's how he would sign his letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm referring to adjudicated facts 1266 that says: In late March 1992 at the session of the Doboj Municipal Assembly the president of the Doboj SDS Ninkovic proposed a division of Doboj town, the division was debated again at a meeting, et cetera, et cetera. By Ninkovic, JNA garrison commander; Cazim Hadzic; his deputy mayor, Stankovic; and Borislav Paravac, president of the SDS. So my question is: Is this the Stankovic that organised these detachments? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not familiar with this Stankovic individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps to clarify, could you tell us what was the relationship between Major Stankovic and the JNA garrison commander you mentioned to us earlier, Cazim?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the general feeling was that he had been sent over from a superior command, that nobody should dare do anything against him. That was the feeling I got from Cazim when these joint patrols were being discussed. People complained of what Stankovic was doing. Cazim said, He doesn't belong with my unit; I don't know who he belongs with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friend. Maybe in answer to His Honour Judge Delvoie, actually, what you just read, it's said that Stankovic was a "major," like rank, but deputy "mayor" is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I think that clarifies the relationship between Mr. Hadzic and Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the unit you say that came from Banja Luka, can you develop on that, please? What was their numbers? If they had a leader?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: They probably had a leader. I can't remember exactly. There were probably 15 or 20 men. As far as I could see, they were directly with Andrija Bjelosevic. I don't know what they did and what their task was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if it was a regular police unit?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Their unit -- you mean this special unit, whether it was a regular unit? I don't know about that. I don't know whether they were members of the regular police or Special Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You just called them, "you mean the special unit;" do you know in any way what was their status?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Judging by their uniforms and the weapons they had, they looked like members of special units. Whether they actually were, I don't know. And I don't know what they did and why they had come. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us about their uniform?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: They also had camouflage uniforms. The only difference was that they all had to wear red berets, red caps. As for the rest, they just had camouflage uniforms. And I don't remember what kind of caps they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm slightly confused here. You said, "The only difference was that they all had to wear red berets, red caps." And then you said, "I don't remember what kind of caps they had." Could you clarify that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, what I said about red berets was that they all had to have red caps. All those who had been recruited were issued red caps immediately and that is how we recognised members of the red berets. Whereas the other members had -- I mean, people from Banja Luka had camouflage uniforms, but I don't remember what their caps looked like. They were definitely not red.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that on the 3rd of May you had seen that members of your police station, Bosniaks and Croats, were arrested. Can you describe to us what was the situation in the police station on the day of the take-over?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: They were arrested already during the night. When I arrived I heard who had been in the station during the night. All the Muslims and Croats were incarcerated, and the people who were guarding the building on the 3rd of May were all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that before the conflict the commander of the police was Irfan Hadzic. What happened to him after the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he remained in his village of Miljkovac. He never appeared at the SUP because it was a suburban neighbourhood of the town where he lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was there a new commander appointed after the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the 2nd of May, pursuant to Stankovic's order, a detachment of police was set up made up of 1300 men. As he said, this detachment was similar to Martic's unit which practically meant that everybody should be transferred from the army to police. They were divided into companies which is not a standard practice in the police. Thirteen companies all in all were established at the time and commanders appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that this was on Stankovic's order, but you are saying he is creating police detachments. What was the CSB chief's role in all this?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he had no role whatsoever because before the war we had reserve police stations scattered around villages, but now he turned all these stations into companies, increased the number of men from the army, and because the army through the Ministry of Defence concerned the people who were detachment, particularly those stationed in town, I think that the entire unit that was formed in that way in town was made up of people who were transferred from the army to the police, therefore, there was no reaction from the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to get at. You say there was no reaction from the CSB. What was the relationship between Mr. Bjelosevic and Mr. Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've never heard of any conflicts arising between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you hear whether Mr. Bjelosevic objected to this way of proceeding?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter 852, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is a report signed by Milos, and I believe you hadn't seen this document at the time, but I would like you to focus on the first paragraph, and it deals with the take-over of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, this is tab 30 on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the screen, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in the middle of the paragraph it deals with a large number of private houses, mainly by Muslim and Croat citizens, suffered serious damage. Described searches and arrests that was incorrect by the so-called Special Forces. And it goes on to describe the units involved including the Special Forces from Banja Luka and Special Forces organised by Bozovic. Is that an accurate reflection of the events as you saw them in early May 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, most problems were caused by these units, various units. There were other units as well, but the most serious problems were caused by the Red Berets and these groups that entered houses, took away their possessions, abused people, and took people to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, I know you haven't seen this document before. We have information that this type of information was written by the national security in Banja Luka. Can you tell us who have access -- how they would have access to this information? How would Banja Luka have access to this type of information in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't seek to tender this document at this time. We can mark it for identification, as we will have somebody to talk about the authenticity of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1337 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we display on the screen 65 ter 3081, which is at tab 21 of the list. If we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is what appears to be a payroll from the Doboj CSB. Do you recognise the name of the chief there?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And we see assistant chief Milan Savic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, when was he appointed assistant chief to Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in May. I think so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Of what year, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this is the CSB Doboj's forensic service. Do you recognise the names on this list?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were these people that were members of the forensic service in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we now go to page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is the first name on that list?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Karagic, who was a member of the Red Berets who were recruited. And this Red Beret unit was under Bozovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this -- these names appear on the payroll of CSB Doboj. Could you tell us what was the relationship between the Red Berets and the chief of the CSB Andrija Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was in command of the Red Berets. I hadn't heard about any disagreements or conflicts between Andrija Bjelosevic and the Red Beret commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And as we were flipping through these pages, this appears to be a payroll for the month of April 1992. Do you agree that on this list -- well, this list is made of mainly Serb police officers, starting from the first page, the pages that we saw earlier?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge is this a list that was -- that emerged from the CSB services? Was it created by the CSB services?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that this list -- actually, every month the reserve police and the centre received salaries from Sarajevo. Since on the night between the 2nd and the 3rd all communications lines with Sarajevo were severed, then these people who were recruited in May were all given salaries for the month of April. That was a decision taken by the staff who had funds available at the time. That was the Crisis Staff. And the funds were provided by the public auditing service. So if we had received funds from Sarajevo for the month of April, this list wouldn't have looked like this because these men were not staff members of the CSB in April but were, rather -- the unit was formed after the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I ask for this document to be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1338, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We saw the name of Slobodan Karagic on that list. Can you tell us about him. Who was he in Doboj in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: He immediately joined the Red Berets, and he was a commander one of these units. And he caused a lot of problems around Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What kind of -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: He went into people's flats and there were complaints about his behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you say he went into people's flats, what kind of complaints were they? What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he would bring in non-Serbs, he would take money from them, he would arrest them without any warrant at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you say he would arrest them; where would he take them to?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: He would take them probably or maybe to the SUP prison or to the army. I don't know where he took them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we display on the screen P1301 MFI. Tab 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, while we are waiting, can I ask the witness, he says about this pay list that this list would -- would not have looked the same -- would not have looked like this because these men were not staff members of the - just one moment - were not staff members of the CSB in April, but the unit -- but rather the unit was formed after the 2nd of May. Does that mean that after the 2nd of May this unit -- these people were staff members of the CSB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were specifically Karagic's Red Berets. I don't know who they were subordinated to. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But they were on the CSB pay list; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, looking at the -- another pay list on the screen - I'm not going to spend too much time on this - do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is a criminal investigation service or section.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you recognise the names on this list?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I have no other questions on this document. If I can ask that to be admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we display 65 ter 3532, please. That's tab 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can we just have the exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was MFI'd. Now it's the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will remain P1301.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a list from the SJB, and we can see your name on the first row. Looking at this list, was this the composition of your SJB?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Maybe if you can scroll down for the witness and also go to the next page in the B/C/S version for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are these the names of the staff members of your police station after May 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions on this document. Can I ask for it to be admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1339, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told us that people were arrested. Can you tell us, on the 3rd of May what do you know about the arrests in the municipality of Doboj?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, if this is a new line, perhaps it's convenient to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on to the next topic, I'd like to show one more payroll which was MFI P1311, please. Tab 26. Can we go to the next page, please. This is not the right document, I apologise. Maybe it's my mistake. This used to be 65 ter 2397. In my records it's P1311. This is not the document that I have here. Right. That's the one. Is this correctly recorded as P1311 MFI?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, it's -- the 65 ter number is right, the P number is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What is the P number, please? 1300, I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P number is 1300, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. MFI, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I apologise for this. Can you tell us what it said at the top of the page in relation to the name of the unit. It's Petar Ceta Milicija, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: This means that there is a detachment in Doboj which has a company. I think that the detachment had 13 companies, in fact, and this is one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S version can we turn to page 3, please. I apologise, page 4, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Under number 83, do you recognise the name?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: 83? Oh, yes, Nikola Jorgic, yes. Yes, I know, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us about Nikola Jorgic and his role in 1992 in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: He was convicted in Germany. He also led a group that was involved in arrests and whatnot, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, he was a member of this Special Police detachment in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: According to this list, he was a member of that detachment. As I said, Stankovic took on all the people and placed them in the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could I ask for that document to be admitted, Your Honours. It's an MFI right now, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So it will remain as Exhibit P1300, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were telling us about the arrests of non-Serbs in Doboj. Next to the police station, is it correct that there was a district prison?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, we have heard and we have evidence that hundreds of people were held there. Was this something that you knew at the time?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Initially I didn't know how this was done. Later on I came to know that after 3.00 they would bring in these people to the detainees and they would beat them up. Whereas during working hours, they would take out individual people, bring them over to the SUP premises for interrogations, beatings, and then take them back to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you are saying "they," who would arrest these people?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Initially it was these groups, mostly; namely, the Red Berets. Later on, Martic's men, when they arrived; Jorga's Group; Karaga's Groups; Preda's Group; they were the ones involved in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let's just go one by one to have the record clear. When you say Martic's men, who are -- who is this group? Can you describe this group?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was after the 15th or the 20th of May that Martic came from Krajina, in other words, it's the Krajina police. They were supposed to take part in the breakthrough of the corridor, and they were stationed in Doboj as were all the other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you say Martic's men from Krajina police, could you just for the benefit of the Trial Chamber tell us where in Krajina they came from? Was this from Bosnia? Where was this from?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's the Krajina in Croatia. The unit came to Doboj, led by Martic, in order to break through a corridor in the direction of Brcko. They were stationed in Doboj, and some of the members of that unit were involved in the arrests, rapes, and mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to have the record clear, when you say Martic, you mean Milan Martic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you said Jorga's Group; who did you mean by Jorga?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Nikola Jorgic from the village of Kostajnica nearby had a group which was part of the army before the war or, rather, before the 2nd of May; and then after the 2nd of May they were again part of the army. And once all of this was over, they were this police detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you said Karaga's Group; and who do you mean by Karaga?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the 2nd of May, Karaga underwent training with the Red Berets. In other words, he was a member of the Red Beret and was under their command, that's to say, under Rajo Bozovic's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was Karaga's full name, just for the record?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan. Slobodan Karagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that people were taken out and beaten up, et cetera, at the district prison. Did you know the ethnic background of the people who were detained in the prison?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Most of them were Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge were these people given any reasons for their arrest and detention?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Initially, no. They would beat them up and take them to the prison and leave them there without any papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you say "initially," did that change?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we first tried to make sure that at least we have drawn up a list of those who were held in the prison, and then to make note of individuals when they were released or taken away from the prison by someone, at least to have a record of who was taken and by whom. There were even incidents related to interventions from the police who wanted to prevent beatings. We even said that the deputy commander of the police station Djeric was beaten up in the process of trying to prevent these beatings on the part of the Red Beret. A couple of months later, a commission was set up which conducted screening of these people and practically released them. It was only after that date, in my view, that proper criminal reports were filed against those who were indeed suspects. And it was then up to the court to try those who were indeed responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you have any interaction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, could we just clarify with the witness. When you said that there was a commission set up to investigate the events in the prison and then you went on to say that they were ultimately released, who did you refer to? The detainees? Or the members of the Red Beret who had been detained during the investigation? Or perhaps a better question would be simply: Were any members of the Red Berets detained during the commission's inquiry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of the Red Berets having been detained. What I was saying was that the Bosniaks and Croats who were held prisoner there, they were screened by the commission ultimately when it was formed, and they would be released at the end of that process because it turned out that they were taken into custody for no reason whatsoever, without any documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, when was this commission established?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the end of June, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I have a document that deals with that. I'll bring it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One more question, please. The witness said that - just one moment, please. "We even said that the deputy commander of the police station Djeric was beaten up in the process of trying to prevent these beatings." Can I have the first name of this deputy commander, Djeric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zoran Djekic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when you came to learn about the conditions in the prison, did you have any interaction with the staff members of the prison or the leadership of the prison?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I probably did. I was aware of the fact, however, that the prison administration was unable to do anything unless everyone was behind the effort. That's why the Crisis Staff set up a commission, because apparently at this level there was no possibility to prevent the goings-on in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did -- who was your -- who was it that you were in contact with in the prison?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I probably spoke to the prison warden or he spoke to me and we probably informed those higher up. We wanted to put a stop to what had been going on by then as soon as possible, because by that time it had been going on for two months perhaps, or even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you are saying that you were in contact with the prison warden, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Milan Vidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you are saying that you tried to report this up. Was the administration of the CSB aware of what was happening in the prison?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think that everyone was aware of that. We were in the same building, and all these people in the building were able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you ask for your superior, the CSB chief, to take any measures in relation to what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably I did. Everybody was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge was any measures taken by the CSB?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. The Red Berets who belonged to I don't know who, they would come to the SUP, to the ground floor level, and they would bring along an individual, beat him up, and then take him to the prison facility which was right behind. If an individual, a Serb, came to pick up his identification documentation or something else, they would even force him to join the beating up of that other individual that was brought along with them. And if such an individual refused to do so, they would beat him up too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you are saying that this was on the ground floor. Where was the office of the CSB chief?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Which floor would that be?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: First floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you are saying that beatings occurred on the ground floor. Was this something that could have been heard on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It could be heard not only on the first floor but on the second floor and outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to display Exhibit P1305, please, which is number 34 on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've seen this document, I believe. It is from the 12th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we scroll to the bottom of the document in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Andrija Bjelosevic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in this document he prohibits arbitrary entry into the premises of the district prison in Doboj as well as the use of physical intimidation and physical force against imprisoned and detained persons; therefore, by the 12th of June it appears that Mr. Bjelosevic knew what was happening in the prison. What can you tell us about the circumstances in which this order was issued?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably what followed next was the setting up of the commission I mentioned, but that was a month and a half later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Other than this order being issued, do you know if any other measures were taken by the CSB to prevent mistreatment in the prison?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what was done specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was a security detail ordered to protect the entrance of the prison?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And we are seeing that this order is being issued by Andrija Bjelosevic. To whom is this being addressed to? This document doesn't seem to say.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. The prison perhaps. The intention may have been for the prison to be able to show this piece of paper to those who engaged in this sort of activity in the prison so that they stopped doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did this piece of paper have any effect?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it had any effect on the Red Berets. I don't know who it was the Red Berets were answerable to. I know that once the commission was set up the situation gradually returned to normal, but in the early days it was chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you said you don't know to whom the Red Berets were answerable to. Can you tell us what was the relationship between the Red Berets chief Bozovic and the CSB chief Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think they were in any sort of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You wrote reports about the behaviour of these groups?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we display 65 ter 3535, please, which is at tab 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is that your signature under your name?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is this one of the reports you wrote?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this report is dated the 12th of August, 1992, and the subject seems to be "Cars stolen in Doboj since the beginning of the war." And you are saying here that a number of cars were driven away by members of the special units from Banja Luka, and the most part of them was taken by members of the Red Beret. Now, looking at the cover page, you sent this to the CSB chief; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And these -- this document specifically deals with the issue of stolen vehicles. Did you write any other reports about other type of crimes committed by these groups?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. In this document you refer to a person by the name of Riki who drove off to Serbia with a Mitsubishi car owned by Ibrahim Sehic. Can you tell us who Riki was?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. This was information from the criminal investigation service. These were their nicknames. What their actual names were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this type of order, would it have -- this type of report, I apologise, would it have reached the desk of the CSB chief?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think this reached the CSB chief Andrija Bjelosevic. It was intended for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And would this sort of information have to be reported up the chain of command in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It would have had to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I ask for this document to be admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1340, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, to your knowledge, were the events in Doboj, specifically about the detention and mistreatment you described in the prison, was that reported above the CSB to the MUP administration?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think that the centre should have known about that because the prison was in the same building where the station and the centre were accommodated, including the national security. We were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And would the section of national security have to report this type of information as well?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I suppose it should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could I ask for P590 to be displayed, please. Tab number 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document that was issued by the CSB in Doboj and dated the 27th of July, and it deals with the problems arising from the activities of paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this document is admitted, so I'll go to page 3 in the English and the B/C/S version. Can we go to the next page. Actually, that's page 5 in e-court for the B/C/S version. The last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see towards the end that there's a discussion about a commission being formed at the Crisis Staff level consisting of representatives of Doboj SJB, CSB, the Red Cross, the Crisis Staff, judicial and military organs, and describes the task. Is this the commission that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And it says that the commission will finish its work by 27 July 1992. And we see what their tasks are: to determine the conditions, the reasons for the capture and detention, the degree of their responsibility, conditions of accommodations, and establish the application of the order on the application of the Rules of International Law. Were you a member of this commission?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know who on behalf of the Doboj SJB or CSB participated in this commission?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in doing these tasks, it appears that they have to finish their work by the 27th of July. You told us that people were released. To your knowledge, when did people start being released from the prison?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, these people for whom there were no criminal reports, the commission decided to set them free. As for those for whom there were criminal reports, they waited for a response to come from the prosecutor and the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We'll get to criminal reports in a moment. We see here that the Crisis Staff was part of this commission. Was the Crisis Staff informed of the condition or did they know about the conditions in the prison as of the moment of the detention, as of the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. The Crisis Staff seemed more to me like an organ assisting, because Stankovic said that he was the commander of town, he issued orders, and, therefore, the Crisis Staff and we from the police even asked our salaries and food and everything from these units and they gave it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: By virtue of your position, were you a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know. I may have gone to see them when we had problems with salaries and other issues that the Crisis Staff could resolve such as fuel supply and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So you attended meetings with the Crisis Staff, but you are saying that you don't know if you were a member of the Crisis Staff. Can you help us understand this?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that I attended these meetings regularly. I only went to the Crisis Staff whenever there was some requirement for the police, as I mentioned, the food, the supplies that were needed by the police, the salaries, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And to your knowledge were members of the Crisis Staff and president of the Crisis Staff, were they aware of the conditions in the prison and the events that you described to us, taking out of detainees, beatings, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. They probably did know, but I'm saying again that Stankovic was the commander of the defence of the town which is something that I didn't see in other towns, and he acted accordingly as being in charge of the Crisis Staff, the police, the army, everyone. Now, I don't know exactly how long it lasted because a few months later Stankovic went away and Simic came who was the commander of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are not sure whether the witness says "operations group."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You have to clarify the last part of your answer. Simic was the commander of what unit?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Simic came -- Lieutenant-Colonel Simic came and became commander of Doboj Operations Group, as it was called. And he was succeeded by General Lisica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And what was Simic's first name, please?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think that he was Lieutenant-Colonel Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned to us earlier that the CSB chief would have to report these events to the MUP. Did you actually know what was his relationship with the higher levels of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that during the period where there was no communication with the corridor or the lines were bad, but after the corridor was opened up, communication opened up as well between the minister and the CSB chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge did the CSB chief attend meetings with the higher-ranking members of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: He probably did, but I don't remember knowing anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of any meetings that he had to attend to and whereby he needed information about the situation in your police station? Would he request information from you to attend such meetings?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: He would probably issue an order to us to furnish him with this kind of information, but he probably never specified for what purpose he needed this information. However, we did provide the information required, and he probably informed the minister thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You are saying "probably." Are you aware of occurrences where Bjelosevic left Doboj to go either to Pale or Bijeljina? Is that something that you remember from that time?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did the CSB chief have regular meetings with his subordinated SJB chiefs?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So from the -- let's start with prior to the war. In 1991, would there be regular meetings between the CSB chief and the SJB chiefs?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, before the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
