utterances.text: And can you explain to us how it is that prior to when there were such meetings and as of, I guess, the month of May there were no such meetings?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the centre chief set up station, for example, in Derventa and Petrovo. There were problems in Teslic. He was probably on the ground a lot of time and he had one-on-one talks with the chiefs there. So he seldom held regular meetings that he used to hold every month, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I see. To your knowledge did he have any contact with the SJB chiefs on the ground? Did he go to these municipalities you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think he did. There were a lot of problems in those municipalities, and he would go there. The chiefs of the stations would be installed. So he spent a lot of time in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did he go to the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Probably. He visited all the municipalities. However, when he went or how many times he went, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing the chief of the SJBs coming to Doboj to visit the CSB chief?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Earlier you mentioned to us that the commission released those prisoners against whom there were no criminal reports. Are you aware of situations where criminal reports were drafted against the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think that those detainees for whom there were criminal reports remained in detention on the prosecutor's orders. As for the rest who didn't have any criminal reports filed against them, they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, what type of crimes were these people generally accused of? And I'm talking about people who were in detention in the district prison, those non-Serbs that you mentioned earlier. First of all, were there criminal complaints against the detainees in the prison?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The reports were filed for possession of fire-arms, for undermining the system, and things like that. Also for divulging information or of their being members of an organisation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You say "for undermining the system;" what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It probably referred to Yugoslavia, but, at the time, Bosnia was recognised, and anyone who was against Yugoslavia was undermining the state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So you're saying that somebody who was against Yugoslavia -- and you're saying that Bosnia was recognised. Can you just clarify what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I said that Bosnia was recognised on the 6th of March, but nevertheless they acted according to the law of Yugoslavia, which stipulates that if you are against, I don't know, the army, the JNA, that would mean that you were against Yugoslavia and you would therefore be committing a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Again, it is the bit that you said about "... at the time, Bosnia was recognised, and anyone who was against Yugoslavia ..." So are you saying that anyone who was for Bosnian's independence was considered to be against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I think that's how it's been formulated in the criminal reports. Anyone who voted for independence of Bosnia ended up with a file -- report filed against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we display P1300 marked for identification, tab 28, please. It's P1311. I see the numbers have been reversed with the previous document. So it's P1311 marked for identification. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us if you've seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mean this case file?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Not this covering page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, it says here that it's issued by the public security station in Doboj and addressed to the public prosecutor's office in Doboj. And it's a criminal report filed against the individuals named here. Now, the first person named here is Senad Mesic. We can see the other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to pay attention to the names and their ethnicity, if you can tell.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: They are Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In the English version, if we can go to page 4. And in the B/C/S version that would be page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, we see here that -- we are still waiting for the B/C/S version to come up. Very well. Can you see here that it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can scroll down in the B/C/S version a little bit, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: -- that this criminal file is based on Article 119 of the Criminal Code of SFRY. Are you familiar with criminal reports being issued under this article of the Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: This was drafted by the criminal investigation service, probably following certain instructions. So I didn't analyse any specific criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You are saying "following certain instructions." Whose instructions would these be, and what instructions are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Probably the instructions relating to how these criminal reports are drafted, and that should be based on the Criminal Code. At the time, Republika Srpska applied the SFRY Criminal Code, and the police inspector who drafted this made reference to this law, and I suppose that the prosecutor and the court worked on the same basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can go to page 7 in the B/C/S version, and it's also page -- page 8 in the English version, I believe. No, it's -- in the B/C/S version can we go back one page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Chief of the criminal investigation service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And on this date, which is the 18th of May, who was the chief of the criminal investigation service?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mladen Vulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Would this type of document reach your desk?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you informed that such criminal reports were being compiled?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I knew that they were being submitted and I knew that if a criminal report is submitted it depended on the prosecutor and the court, whether the prosecutor would reject this criminal report if it was flawed, and if it was not written properly by this person here, and the people concerned would have no problems consequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us of examples where people were being investigated for having voted for the independence of Bosnia. What did you make of these investigations and criminal reports at the time?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: A criminal report is filed to the district prosecutor, and if it is accepted by the prosecutor, it's then forwarded to the court. If not, the people would be released from detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could I ask for this document which was MFI'd to be entered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, but could we just clarify a few things in relation to the jurisdiction of these crimes, because I noted that in the document, the group, Mr. Zenad Mesic and others, were being suspected of having committed crimes against the army according to Article 119 of the Criminal Code. My question is: Wouldn't that fall under the jurisdiction of the military courts?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you heard the Honourable Judge's question. What can you say about the jurisdiction of the civil courts on these matters?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was under the jurisdiction of military court, but at that time there were no military courts set up as yet. And probably at some higher level of authority, and maybe from the centre, ordered, given that the military prosecutor and the courts were not in operation as yet, to do that. I do know that a number of cases were then transferred to the military courts once they were established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And when were the military courts set up in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You were requesting the deMFIcation of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As it remains, P1311, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, still in the issue of the detainees in the district prison, were you aware that policemen, investigators from the MUP, were taking prisoners out of the prison for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I probably knew about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And were you aware of occurrences of physical force being applied on the detainees by members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard that there were MUP members who applied force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was -- to your knowledge these were members of which section of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The -- must have been done by members of the criminal investigation service. Should have been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Of the SJB or the CSB, if you know?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Both from the station and the centre. Both were involved in these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At the beginning of the day today you mentioned that on the day of the take-over the Muslim and Croat members of your police station were arrested and detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we display on the screen P1315, please. Tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a log-book obtained from the prison -- from the district prison in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you see the individual at number 67 -- I apologise, number 64?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was about the individual Mirza Lisinovic who was arrested on that night between the 2nd and 3rd and was taken to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know how long he was detained in the prison?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if any -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think for a month perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if anything happened to him while he was in detention?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: He was beaten up. Later on he was released. And I know he is alive and well living in Sarajevo now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you go down to 84, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name at number 84?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Refik Buljubasic. Policeman. I don't know when he was detained but I do know that he was detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was his role in the police station?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think he was an ordinary policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if you go up two names, number 82?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Karlo Grgic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I did. He used to be a commander. Then in 1991 or 1992 he was assistant commander, I believe. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say assistant commander, which organisation was he a member of?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the pre-war period, the general police station where Irfan was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I understand. Do you know what happened to him while he was in detention, Mr. Grgic?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I heard that the Red Berets had taken him somewhere and killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can put this document away for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, other than the district prison in Doboj, do you know of other detention centres that were being maintained at the time in Doboj, as of the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: There was the military prison at Usora, military prison at Bare. The Red Berets held a prison facility near Perca.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What is this prison facility near Perca?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It was a camp that they had on the road to Sarajevo. It was a private home that was turned into a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us of a military prison in Usora, at Bare. Were you aware also of a disco used as a detention centre?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's what I meant when I said Perca; that was the Percin Disco that was kept by the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge were there any interrogations taking place at Percin's Disco?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think that there were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you know whether any inspectors from the MUP participated in these interrogations?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of inspectors from the MUP, from the MUP headquarters, visiting Doboj during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we display 65 ter 1274. Tab 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This document is dated the 12th of August. It is a report to the minister. If we go to page 3, you can see that it is -- under the signature block you have the name of Milos Zuban, chief of police. Did you know Mr. Zuban?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if we go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this document refers to meetings held in August with Andrija Bjelosevic in the presence of Mirko Blazanovic. Do you remember Mr. Blazanovic?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And it discusses the issues, the work of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If you go to, in the English version, the second page. And in the B/C/S version also the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the second paragraph which deals with the selection of candidates for the employment in the police. And in the middle of the paragraph it talks about the reserve police team being currently reduced and examined in order to correspond to real current needs, and it mentions you here. Can you tell us in which context this issue arose?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had 1300 policemen, which wasn't usual at all. We were more of a military unit than a police force in that context. The minister probably ordered that the numbers be reduced, which we probably did. Reserve police stations were to be set up again, and the surplus staff were assigned to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember being informed about this order from the minister, from the ministry, and how was it conveyed to you?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I probably received a written order, as did the other stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And who would you receive this written order from?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Probably the centre chief. If the minister addressed this to the chief of the centre, then he would receive it, and he would in turn write letters to the chiefs of stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I won't seek to tender this document at this time. We will have a witness to talk about it. If we could just mark it for identification at this point, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1341 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I be excused just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we display, please, Exhibit 1D00072, please. Tab 69 on the list. This is not it. 1D00072. That's the one. This is not the document that I seek to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps we can take the break at this point, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It is there. If I can just ask him very quickly, since we've pulled it up now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, just as an order by the Ministry of the Interior about submitting daily incident bulletins, and it's addressed to all CSBs. Do you remember on what frequency you were submitting reports to your CSB?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What was the normal way of proceeding with reports to the CSB? How frequently were you to report to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. Based on these dispatches, well, we had to send reports. Now, whether it was the service, the administrative department, or the police detachment, but I do believe that we sent reports on a regular basis pursuant to the orders from the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Might be a suitable time to take the break now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we resume, I note for the record that we reconvene for this last session under Rule 15 bis, Judge Harhoff being absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you mentioned to us earlier the Special Police detachment. I would like you to look at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Which is 65 ter 2387, at tab 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It's a report on the activities of the Doboj Police Detachment dated the 5th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, before we look at the document, could you please -- could we go to the last page, to the signature block, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Detachment commander Bosko Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The document is -- the header of the document seems to suggest that it is from the CSB Doboj, and it is written in Doboj on the 5th of September, 1992. Do you know if this document would have been sent up the chain of command? To was this document -- for whom was this document drafted?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The detachment was set up immediately following the 2nd of May, and was -- this was probably sent to the Doboj CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to page 3 in the B/C/S version and page 4 in the English version. I apologise, page 3 in the English version, which is also page 3 in the B/C/S version. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, first of all, do you see the initial paragraph which says that the Doboj Police Detachment was formed on the 8th of May, initially consisted of 1300 police officers, which you were telling us about earlier, and the detachment was re-organised and the number was reduced to 720. Is that an accurate reflection of the events back then?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The next paragraph says that a total of 184 active and reserve police officers participated in the liberation of Doboj and that the entire police force together with the Serbian army has taken part in fights on the northern front, et cetera. Is that also an accurate reflection of the events?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the night between the 2nd and the 3rd, as far as I know it was only the Red Berets who had taken control of the centre. The police force probably took part in the subsequent activities. It could definitely not have had 184 active members since after the second of the 100 active servicemen who should have been there, there were maybe 30 of them. Now, this could have been the case only when the manpower was 1300. After the 3rd, the army subordinated all of the police stations that were within its area of responsibility in order to engage them in combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: A little lower in that paragraph it deals with special combat on the 12th of July, and it deals with the southern front. Do you know anything about these events?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, the BH Army attacked these lines, breached them, and advanced toward the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And on the 12th of July, is that a day that sticks out for you?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I know that the lines were breached. That was when the Red Berets were attacked because they were stationed along the line where combat took place. That's where their camp was. It was for this reason that what ensued was --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, continue. I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Incidents occurred concerning human shields and all the other problems that were present in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, what do you know about this human shields incident?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Based on what I heard later on, the BH Army attacked the area where the Red Berets were billeted. I think that two members of the Red Berets were killed. As a result, based on my understanding of these events, the Red Berets took out the individuals detained in the disco and used them as human shields and that's how they came to be killed along that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, are you saying the Red Berets took out these individuals; was it only the Red Berets that were involved in this event?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think that they were in charge. Now, as for others, if there were members of the army present, they would have taken them along too and if there were policemen in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The document here says that the police is engaged on the southern front. To your knowledge were they also involved in these events?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: They probably didn't take part directly there. If there was a reserve police station in the area, it was subordinated to the army and together they defended the general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to page 5 in the English version, which is page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And under item L, Mr. Petrovic, we see some statistics here. For example, it says here that the Special Police detachment was involved in 17 convoys escorted. Do you happen to know what these convoys consisted of?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps these were convoys heading from Bijeljina and Serbia toward Banja Luka carrying fuel and food. As soon as the corridor opened up, large convoys set off toward the Krajina, that's to say, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Below that we see a number of facilities secured by the police. It says 12. Do you know what facilities the police were securing in the town of Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. The municipality building, banks, post offices, the railway station, the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And now, this is the document that you say was signed by Mr. Bosko Djukic. He is the individual you referred to earlier on today?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. I was talking about Zoran Djekic, who was assaulted. He was the assistant commander, whereas this other one was the detachment commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I ask for this document to be admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1345, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, did you know an individual by the name of Milutin Blaskovic?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber who this person was?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Up until 1991, Milutin Blaskovic was the chief of police at the public security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what happened in 1991?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: He was retired. And then in 1992 he was mobilised and joined the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And for how long was he in the police force, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Before the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: After the war, in 1992. Sorry, during the war. When you said he was mobilised, how long was he ...

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: From 1992 through to the end of the war in 1995, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. You were mentioning to us the Red Berets. I'd like to look -- I'd like you to look at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: 65 ter 3082, which is at tab 22, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is another payroll from the CSB and it indicates that this is a special group. Can you tell us more about this document?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is a group that arrived from Ozren. Save for Radojica Bozovic, I think all the other ones are not real people. And I think Radojica is the only authentic name. But they had their nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And why is it that you say that the other ones are not real people?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think anyone knew their names. Only their nicknames were used. And what happened here is -- well, that's an assumption on my part, because I don't think they were able to learn their names. And I know that it was strictly forbidden for anyone to inquire after their names. And I don't believe at all that these are their genuine names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Other than the person at position number 1, Radojica Bozovic; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you talked about Radojica Bozovic, you were saying that he was the leader of the Red Berets; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge was he and his unit paid by the CSB Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Based on this, I can see that they all received their pay in Doboj. I can see that even those who were from Banja Luka, they received their monies in Doboj. So it must have been the case that the Crisis Staff earmarked funds for their pay. And I can see that even at this time when they were not in Doboj but rather up at Ozren they received their salaries there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can I ask Your Honours to admit this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1346, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I'd like you to look at another document which is P405. Tab 58. In the B/C/S version -- well, let's leave it there for now. This is a report from the 22nd of October, 1992, the Ministry of Interior in Bijeljina, about a visit to the CSB in Doboj and the SJBs within the Doboj CSB. On the first page in B/C/S, and that's the second page in English, there's a discussion about the reduction of members of the SJB. And here we can read that: "The CSB chief believes that the reduction should have taken place, but it seems that the SJB management does not wish to implement this decision." Can you explain to us the circumstances surrounding this issue?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I suppose that it wasn't easy of that number of people who were at the station to have a reduction. For example, if you have 700 policemen, you should have 300 and the people should be sent to the army after they had been together for six months. Probably why there was resistance to that at the stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At the end of this paragraph they say that the numbers should be reduced to 480 police officers instead of 875. Are those numbers an accurate reflection of what was happening back then?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can go to page 4 in the B/C/S version and page 6 in the English version, we can see the section entitled "Crime Prevention and Detection."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Petrovic? Do you see the second sentence --

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see the second sentence which starts with: "All public security stations were told to emphasise," and we have to go to the next page in English, please, "the documentation of war crimes against the Serbian people ..." Do you remember receiving instructions on documenting war crimes against the Serbian population only?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, we saw the criminal reports filed earlier. We saw one example of criminal reports filed against non-Serbs. Do you know if any criminal reports were filed during the summer of 1992, the end of the year, for any war crimes committed against the non-Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you say you don't remember, you don't remember that any were filed, or you don't remember the topic at all?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if there were any criminal reports of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to move to another topic. In relation to a group which was led by the individual we mentioned before, Milan Savic, could you tell us anything that you know about a certain group that was led by this man?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, Milan Savic worked before the war in the criminal and forensic department, the section which was called counter-subversive. Stankovic had an attachment in town itself, and he was a member of that detachment, but I don't know exactly what his task was. In the meantime, he was appointed assistant chief of the centre. It took place either in April or May; I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when he became assistant chief of the centre, do you know if at that time he created a group that was active in another municipality?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, but he was present in Teslic and in Modrica, and I think that with the Red Berets - but I don't know on whose authority he could issue orders - they went to Teslic and Modrica, he and the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to take a look at 65 ter 2788. Now, this is a document from the CSB in Doboj on the 17th of July, 1992. You were just mentioning Teslic. This was sent to the investigating judge of the Teslic lower court and it is in relation to Dobrivoje Culibrk and others. Do you know Dobrivoje Culibrk?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us about him? What was his role and function in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: He worked in the state security service, and I know only of one instance when he was arrested near Tesanj for transporting explosives. And this is how I remember him before the war. He was subsequently released at the intervention by the army because the army claimed that that was their explosive. I only know that the situation became quite complicated. I know that Culibrk and Milan Savic were good friends before the war, during the war, and after the war. And I even think - I'm not one hundred per cent sure - that this is the signature of Milan Savic. This signature on behalf of the CSB chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that it's signed for the CSB chief here. Now, this document requests the immediate release of Culibrk, then we have a few names: Pijunovic, Tekic, Spasojevic, and Djuric. Did you know these men, besides Culibrk?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know those were men of very dubious characteristics. They were prone to criminality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you know whether this group of men were known under a nickname, whether their group had a name?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I know that they went by the name of Mices or Mice in Teslic. Whether they were actually members of that group, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you know under which circumstances this document was issued? It appears that they are in detention and their release is requested. Do you know anything more about this?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. That was taking place in Teslic. I know that the people were detained and that these men were from Doboj. The chief of the centre and Savic, his assistant, went to Teslic, but what happened up there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you're saying that this signature is probably Mr. Savic's; is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And would the chief of the centre have been aware of this document? Do you know if he was?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what was the relationship between Andrija Bjelosevic and Milan Savic during that time?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. He was a deputy because there was no assistant position at the time so he was a deputy. What their relationship was after the Teslic events, I don't know. I know that they were on good terms before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll hear more about this group and the Teslic, but at this time could I ask for this document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm not sure I appreciate that there's a sufficient nexus between the document and the witness, having regard to his -- what he has said about it. Isn't it somewhat remote from him?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: He knows the individuals in this group. He knows who probably signed it. It was issued from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's putting it rather high when you said "who probably signed it." That was not my understanding of his recognition or non-recognition of the signature, but please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: On the other hand, Mr. Demirdjian, we are talking about an adjudicated fact, 1215. No, sorry, 1216.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In relation to the signature of this document? I know about the group, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In relation to the group, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, but in relation to this letter and the request for release of these individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if Your Honours remember with one of our previous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And in relation to the release of these individuals as well. But perhaps not the document, don't discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I believe the document might corroborate this adjudicated fact and substantiate other -- what other witnesses will say about this event. Now, since this is issued by the CSB of Doboj, and we have the subordinated SJB chief, it might be a good person to tender this document through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Inasmuch as it's -- and I thank Judge Delvoie for point out that this emanates as it were from an adjudicated fact, it's admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1342, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In relation to these events in Teslic, Mr. Petrovic, I would like you to look at 65 ter 865. Which is tab 53. Just for the record it's 65 ter 835 -- 865, I apologise, 865.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is an information on the arrest of a group of persons in Teslic on the 30th of June. And if you scroll down, sir, you will see that that discusses Milan Savic we just talked about. Now, in relation to Savic here, you see that it says: "We would like to mention that Savic was appointed assistant chief of the Doboj CSB on 23 June 1992." Do you -- does this reflect your recollection of the events back then, that this was around the time that he was appointed?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And we see --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And we would need to go to the next page in the B/C/S version and keep the document in English on that page. Another page in the B/C/S version, the next page. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the paragraph that starts with: "On 29 June 1992 when Dobrivoje Culibrk indicated that there were problems and he needed help, Milan Savic sent a group of 15 members of the Red Berets led by Slobodan Karagic." You just mentioned a moment ago that Savic went to Teslic and that he sent Red Berets; is this what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to this, I see that Milan Savic issued an order to the Red Berets commanded by Bozovic. Slobodan Karagic was just a platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we go to the page before last in the B/C/S version, signature block. That's the last page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Does it there have the name of the chief of the centre?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Andrija Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could I ask for that document to be admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1343, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, to your knowledge, what was the relationship, if you know, between the chief of the centre, Mr. Bjelosevic, and the members of this group, the Mice Group?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Mice Group were, in fact, released after these documents were issued?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was it a known fact eventually that the Mice Group was released?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that that was debated and that these men were from Doboj, and, therefore, an attempt was made to create a conflict between Teslic and Doboj on account of these men, but I can't remember if or when they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We've heard that these men were transferred to Doboj, at least some members of this group, and that they were detained in a district prison. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P835, please. Which is at tab 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You can see this is a document that was drafted by the Banja Luka National Security Service. And if you scroll down to the second paragraph, it talks about Colonel Slavko Lisica making it "possible for members of the Mice Group from Doboj, who had previously been arrested, and a Special Police battalion from Doboj to take part in war operations under the command of Andrija Bjelosevic." Were you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: That Andrija was in charge in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The document here at the second paragraph says that the Mice Group were taking part in war operations under the command of Andrija Bjelosevic. First of all, were you aware that Andrija Bjelosevic took part in war operations?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I know that after these events took place, Andrija Bjelosevic went to Teslic because it was under the jurisdiction of the Doboj Centre. I heard of him being arrested as well, but how it all evolved, I don't know. Whether he took part in that, whether he organised something there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. One last question on this issue. This is a document issued in November 1992, and it talks about the fact that this group was previously arrested and that it is now taking part in war operations. Did you know that they were released and they were taking part in war operations; were you aware of that? The Mice Group.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It mentions here Colonel Slavko Lisica. Did you know this colonel?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He came to become a tactical group commander after Simic left, and he was the commander of the Doboj Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see him in Doboj in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did, after he came, towards the end of September or thereabouts. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did he meet with municipal authorities in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He invited the municipal leadership separately, the company manager separately, he called us from the SUP as well, issued orders to us, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned at the beginning of your testimony today that you were the chief of the police station until December 1992 and that you were dismissed at that point. Could you tell the Trial Chamber the circumstances surrounding your dismissal?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, in October there was a meeting held at General Ristic's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: General Lisica office. Witness, please repeat the answer. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: There was a little problem. I would ask you to repeat the answer again, please, because it wasn't properly recorded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: So in October a meeting was held in the office of General Lisica attended by representatives of the centre, namely, Andrija Bjelosevic and someone else - I don't know who. There were also representatives of the municipal authority, the councillors; and a decision was taken to dismiss me from the position of the chief of the station. I didn't know about this meeting. I only heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You were not present at this meeting then?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, that was the first meeting; it was followed by a second one; and I think that somebody from the MUP of Republika Srpska was in attendance as well because I saw the car that belonged to the MUP of Republika Srpska. The meeting was held in the municipal building, and the same people attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When did you find out about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Afterwards. Somebody who attended the meeting told me what the topic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was any reasons for your dismissal provided to you?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was offended by the fact that these meetings were held in secrecy. There was no need for that. They could have invited me, told me the reasons for my dismissal; and they could have quite easily dismissed me provided there were enough grounds for that. However, from what I could see from the written proposal for my dismissal, one of the first reasons was my failure to restore order in the area of Doboj municipality. And also one of the points referred to my providing protection to the Muslims, because a small number of Muslims worked in the municipal building in the police station and the administrative section. And after that all of these people were sacked from their jobs. I believe that I was guilty, but I wasn't the only one of that. However, I was hurt by this dismissal because they never conducted any interview with me. We could have solved it differently. They just dismissed me and transferred me to a different job without any reason whatsoever. After that, I wasn't able to see any room for progress for me. My commander, who was more responsible than I, remained. Therefore, my suspicion that I had at the time will still remain suspicion regarding my dismissal. When I saw that no proper help could be provided, I tried to provide individual help to some Muslims. That's as much as I could do, and I am prepared to answer for everything that I did wrongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You said that the proposal --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I believe page 72, line 4, I believe the witness said "my commander of police."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic, just to clarify the transcript here, it says that "my commander ... was more responsible than I." Is this a correct or accurate reflection of what you just said?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I meant the detachment commander, not my commander. The commander of the police detachment that was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could I have one more clarification, please. Just before that the witness said "I believe that I was guilty, but I was not the only one of that." What did the witness mean by being guilty? Being guilty of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You heard Your Honour's question, if you could answer. What did you feel you were guilty of?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, in my view, what had to be prevented at any cost was the mistreatment and maltreatment of people. In other words, if the Red Berets arrived or if special units arrived from Banja Luka or wherever, my belief was that they were going to contribute to the restoration of law and order, rather than disrupt it. It is difficult for an individual who hails from Doboj to look at the way the events unfold without being able to do anything. And we received interventions and calls from people on a daily basis complaining of abuse, mistreatment, beatings, and one was unable to do anything. You could provide help as an individual, but you couldn't do anything else to ensure protection for these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that these daily occurrences were happening, and you also told us that this was informed -- this information was provided to your superior, your CSB chief; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do believe that reports were written. But let me repeat: This building is located in the centre of Doboj. Everyone was aware of what was going on. You can't tell me that those who were in the police station, the Crisis Staff, the army, that they weren't aware of these events. All of these buildings are located in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And now we are coming to your dismissal. You told us that a proposal was written and sent to the MUP for your dismissal. You didn't tell us who wrote that dismissal -- or that proposal, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Following Lisica's letter, Andrija Bjelosevic drafted the proposal because I believe that it was Lisica who actually got in touch with Andrija Bjelosevic on this issue, and then Bjelosevic wrote a proposal that I be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Who did he send this proposal to?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: To Minister Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what happened after this proposal?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I received a decision on my removal, and I was assigned to the post of desk officer or inspector in charge of aliens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What did the proposal say? Did the proposal also include the reasons for your removal?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. The formulation was, Is hereby removed, and that the responsibility of the chief of the station is to be investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I meant to talk about the proposal that was sent by Bjelosevic. Did that proposal include the reasons for which your dismissal was proposed?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The two reasons you gave us earlier, the management of the police station and assisting Muslims, were those two reasons in the proposal?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I believe so. The first reason was that I did not manage to enforce law and order, the usual stuff. Then under 2, provided protection for Muslims which led to a decline in the morale of the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: After this proposal was sent, you tell us you received the decision. Were you interviewed by anyone in the MUP leadership, in the administration? Was any procedure set into place to hear you?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. That's what I hold against the minister as an individual, the fact that he never heard what I had to say. And then if he thought that what I did was wrong, I would not hold it against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this document, this proposal by Bjelosevic, to your knowledge is it still available today?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think it can be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian -- if I -- perhaps first Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. There is some -- one part is missing in the transcript. It's line 74 [sic] -- page 74, line 90. Because the last part of the witness response missing: He said that were probably the Lisica's proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic -- may I clarify that first, Your Honours? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the answer here which you provided to us about the two reasons. You said then under two, provided protection for Muslims which led to decline in the morale in the police and the army. Was there anything else you said after that, because this is not recorded in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I said that first a meeting was held in October in Lisica's office and that then they sent a letter to the centre and the centre then formulated their proposal to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours had a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. For the witness, I'm still not very clear about the answer about what the witness said about being guilty. You were discussing with the witness his -- the reasons of his dismissal. And he said: "I believe that I was guilty, but I wasn't the only one." And then he said: "The commander of the detachment, who was more responsible than I, remained." So I'm a little bit puzzled about what he means about "I was guilty." Was he -- is he referring to -- Mr. Witness, are you referring to the reason for your dismissal, or are you referring to something else? So, very precisely, what did you mean when you said "I believe that I was guilty"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the statement of reasons given in Lisica's office for my removal. Under one, that I didn't enforce law and order and then that vehicles were stolen during my term of office. I don't know what it was that they wrote. And I said that while these events were taking place, I seem to have been the only one found guilty because I was the only one removed. I wasn't present at the meeting, and I'm not aware of what it was that they discussed, but what I said was that somebody else should have been held accountable as well because all these events took place in the centre. This is what makes me suspicious, the fact that I was the only one to have been removed. And I'm puzzled by this need to remove from office only one individual and that's me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic, I understand now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, in relation to this matter, can you, perhaps, explain to the Trial Chamber what was your relationship with Mr. Bjelosevic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not on good terms with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was there a reason for that? Was there any specific reason why?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think that we had a different approach to work. Before the war, I was a policeman, whereas Andrija Bjelosevic was not. In my view, what was required was more discipline and more work, and I believe that we were capable of doing the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I complete, there's one last topic I'd like to address. And we have under adjudicated facts 1264 the ethnic break-down of the municipality of Doboj which said that 40 per cent were Muslim, before the war, 39 Serb, et cetera. There's one document that I hadn't placed on the list, but I discussed with the Defence during the break, we have the ethnic map of Doboj which we've uploaded as document 10236.06. With Your Honours' leave, I would just like to display that document to the witness and see if he can comments on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I'm about to show you a map of Doboj, I didn't have a chance to show it to you earlier. It is in relation to the municipality of Doboj and the ethnic composition. And this is, I believe, in 1991. Now, we can see that the municipality or the villages or the towns in the municipality are colour coded according to the majority ethnic group. And we can see that there's Bosnian Croats in red, Bosnian Serbs in blue, Bosniaks in green. If you pay attention to this map, would you comment on how accurate this is and if it's an accurate reflection of the ethnic distribution in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I believe it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And to your knowledge, at the end of 1992 and in the following years, did the ethnic composition in the municipality of Doboj -- was it affected by the events in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. However, an important point that needs to be made: Doboj East, that's to say, the area in direction of Tuzla, that's to say, Brezica Velike and Brezica Mala, Lokotnica [phoen], all these settlements in the direction of Tuzla, if you can see them; that's Doboj East. And as of 1992, it no longer was part of Doboj municipality. As for Doboj South, Metuzici [phoen], that stayed with Doboj municipality. As for Alibegovac, Metlovac [phoen], they belonged to Usora municipality. They belong to the Federation as they did back in 1992. All the rest falls under Doboj municipality back in 1992. As for Jahovac and Komarica, they were populated by Croats who left in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I was mentioning earlier that it is an admitted facts in this case that according to the 1991 census the municipality was made of 40 per cent Muslims, 39 per cent of Serbs; what was the impact of the conflict on these percentages?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: As I've just said, if you take Doboj East and Doboj South and Usora staying as they are, nobody moved out -- well, all the other areas in the municipality, the population largely moved out, and only a small percentage remained until the end of the war in 1995 when the population gradually started returning to the area. Well, roughly, there were 40.000 Bosniaks; 20.000 remained in Doboj East and Doboj South; and 20.000 remained in Doboj town and surroundings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, would you repeat the last part of your sentence. The interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC
utterances.text: There was a total of 40.000 Bosniaks; that's before the war. 20.000 Bosniak stayed behind in Doboj East, South, and Usora; and 20.000 remained in the area of Republika Srpska, that is to say, the rest of the Doboj municipality. Now, as for -- so just a small percentage, a small fraction, remained during the war, and a large majority moved out and stayed out until the end of the war. So I said roughly 20.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you are telling us that roughly 20 -- of the 20.000 -- can you clarify to us by the end of the war what was, roughly speaking, the percentage of Bosniaks and Croats left in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, wouldn't it be easier to stay with numbers now, rather than percentages? We have -- the witness said there were 20.000 in Doboj Centre before the war; 20.000 other ones in south and east, and they stayed; and if I understand it well, most of the 20.000 in Doboj Centre moved out. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and the surrounding places as well. They left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then after the war in 1995, how many did return from those 20.000 who left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Post-2000, all of them returned. That was when the bulk of them returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Your Honours, can I ask for this ethnic map to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1344, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a practical proposal to make. I cannot finish any of the topics that I mean to discuss with the witness in the remaining time, and I suggest that we start our cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Whereas I'm reluctant to waste the 10 minutes, I understand the practicality of your suggestion, Mr. Cvijetic. So we would have to rise now. Mr. Petrovic, you having been sworn as a witness -- thank you, Mr. Cvijetic. Mr. Petrovic, having been sworn as a witness in this matter - as you would have gathered, we are about to take the adjournment - but you having been sworn as a witness, I'm obliged to point out to you that you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side in this matter. And in such conversations as you may have outside of the Chamber, you can't discuss your testimony with anyone. So we will reconvene in this courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
